messages.content: The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I lose my place constantly when I'm reviewing a long contract. By page thirty I can't remember what page four said that contradicted it.

Stop trying to hold the document in your head — that's the wrong tool for the job. Keep a running ledger beside you: clause number, what it commits you to, and any earlier clause it touches. Your memory then only has to carry the ledger, not the contract. Contradictions surface as two rows pointing at each other.

Every time someone interrupts me mid-task I lose about fifteen minutes rebuilding where I was. How do I recover faster?

Leave yourself a breadcrumb before you turn away. One sentence describing the next physical action — not the goal, the action — is usually enough to restore context in seconds rather than minutes. The cost of interruption is mostly reconstruction, so pay a little up front to avoid paying a lot afterward.

I'm juggling four client accounts and I keep mixing up which decisions belong to which. What's the fix?

Externalize the boundaries. Each account needs its own written state — current decision, open question, who owes whom what — and you should read that state before touching the account and update it before leaving. Interference between accounts happens because they share space in memory; give them separate spaces on paper.

I can follow a technical discussion fine, but the moment I have to also take notes I lose the thread entirely.

You're asking one system to do two jobs that compete for the same resource. Record the conversation if you can and listen properly, or capture only trigger words — three or four per topic — that let you reconstruct afterward. Full notes taken live are usually worse than sparse notes plus an intact understanding.

How do I keep track of the six things people asked me for today without writing a novel?

Capture each request as requester, deliverable, deadline. Three fields, one line. The discipline is capturing it at the moment of the ask, not at the end of the day when four of them have already evaporated. Length isn't what makes a list useful; completeness is.

I read a paragraph three times and still don't absorb it when I'm tired. Should I push through?

No — comprehension at that point costs more than it returns. When working memory is depleted, rereading mostly reinforces the failure. Switch to something mechanical, or stop. If the deadline forbids stopping, read with a pen and force yourself to summarize each paragraph in one line; the act of producing output catches what passive reading won't.

My handover notes are always incomplete and my colleague has to ask me five questions afterward.

Write the handover for someone with no context, then delete nothing. The gaps appear because you're compressing against your own knowledge, which the reader doesn't share. A useful test: could they act on this if you were unreachable for a week? If not, the missing pieces are exactly what they'll ask about.

I keep forgetting to follow up on things I promised in meetings.

The failure isn't memory, it's the absence of a capture step. Anything you commit to out loud goes into a single list before you leave the room — not afterward, not into four different apps. Then the only habit you need to maintain is reviewing one list, which is a far smaller thing to sustain than remembering commitments.

I have a product launch in six weeks and no idea where to start. Everything feels equally urgent.

Work backward from the launch date and identify what physically cannot happen until something else finishes. Those dependencies define your critical path, and everything on it is genuinely urgent; everything off it only feels that way. Schedule the path first, then fit the rest into the gaps it leaves.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Two of my tasks each depend on the other being partly done. How do I sequence that?

Split them. Circular dependencies almost always dissolve once you separate the part that's genuinely needed upstream from the part that isn't. Identify the minimum each one needs from the other, deliver those two slices first, then finish both in parallel.

My project plan looks fine on paper but I'm always three days behind by week two.

Your estimates are probably durations, not elapsed time. A task that takes six hours of work doesn't take six hours of calendar — it takes six hours plus interruptions, handoffs, and waiting on other people. Track the ratio between the two for a few weeks and apply it as a multiplier rather than trying to work faster.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How far ahead should I actually be planning?

Far enough to see the dependencies, no further. Detailed plans past the point where your assumptions hold are wasted effort, because they'll be rewritten. A useful shape is: next week in detail, next month in milestones, next quarter in outcomes.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I've been asked to scope a project in an area I don't know well. How do I plan something I don't understand yet?

Plan the learning first as a real task with its own deadline, then scope the work afterward. Committing to estimates before you understand the domain produces numbers everyone treats as promises. A two-day investigation that produces a defensible estimate is worth more than an immediate guess that's wrong by a factor of three.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Our team keeps discovering blocking issues halfway through sprints.

Add a pre-flight step: before work starts, each item gets checked for what it needs from outside the team. Most mid-sprint blocks are dependencies nobody looked for, not genuine surprises. The check takes minutes and it converts a mid-sprint emergency into a scheduling decision made in advance.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I have a long-term goal I keep not making progress on because urgent things always win.

Urgency will always win on a level playing field, so stop making it level. Give the long-term goal a fixed slot that isn't negotiable against same-day requests, and make the next action on it small enough that a bad day doesn't derail it. Progress on long horizons comes from protecting a floor, not from finding large blocks of time.

How do I break down something as vague as 'improve onboarding'?

Turn it into a question you could answer with evidence: where do new people currently get stuck? Then the work becomes finding out — interviews, drop-off points, first-week tickets — and the tasks follow from what you learn. Vague goals resist decomposition because they're missing a diagnosis, not because they're too big.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Is multitasking actually costing me anything or is that a myth?

It costs you real time. Each switch requires loading the new context and suppressing the old one, and the suppression lingers — part of your attention stays on the abandoned task for minutes afterward. Two tasks done sequentially almost always finish sooner than the same two interleaved.

I batch similar work together but I still feel scattered. What am I missing?

Batching by task type isn't enough if the tasks need different mental modes. Writing and reviewing are both 'documents' but they use opposite postures — one generative, one critical — and switching between them is as expensive as switching projects. Batch by the mode the work demands, not by its category.

My mornings are productive and my afternoons are useless. Should I just accept that?

Use it rather than fight it. Put work that needs held context and novel thinking in the morning, and work that runs on established structure — reviews, correspondence, administrative tasks — in the afternoon. You're not making the afternoon better; you're making it matter less.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I get pulled into Slack constantly and can't seem to stop checking it.

The pull is that checking sometimes pays off, which is the hardest pattern to break. Make the cost asymmetric: close it entirely for defined blocks and tell your team what your response window is. Availability that's predictable is more useful to colleagues than availability that's constant but distracted.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Should I finish one project completely before starting the next?

Usually yes, with one exception: when a project has genuine waiting periods you can't compress. Then a second stream is efficient. But two projects both actively demanding decisions will each run slower than they would alone, and the total will exceed doing them in sequence.

I have to switch between deep technical work and management conversations several times a day.

Cluster the conversations. Scattered meetings fragment the day into intervals too short for technical work, even though the total meeting time is modest. Three hours of meetings in one block leaves five usable hours; the same three hours spread across the day leaves almost none.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I start optimizing things that don't matter whenever a task gets hard. How do I stop?

Notice that the switch is doing something for you — it converts an uncomfortable problem into a comfortable one. Name the hard task's next concrete step before you begin, so that when the pull arrives you have something specific to return to. Vague next steps make displacement activities much more attractive.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Halfway through most projects I want to restart with a better approach.

Write the better approach down and keep going. Sometimes it's genuinely better; more often it's the appeal of a clean slate against a half-finished thing. Deciding at the end, with a working version in hand and the alternative documented, gives you a real comparison instead of a hypothetical one.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My team keeps expanding the scope of a project that was supposed to ship last month.

Freeze the definition of done in writing and route every new idea to a list explicitly labeled for the next version. Scope creep survives on ambiguity about what 'finished' means; once that's written down, additions have to argue against a stated boundary rather than filling a vacuum.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How do I stay focused on a goal that won't show results for a year?

Attach it to something you can observe weekly. Long horizons fail because there's no feedback, not because motivation runs out — a leading indicator you can actually move gives you the signal the outcome can't yet provide. Track effort or intermediate output, not the distant result.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I keep saying yes to things and then resenting the workload.

The resentment is information: you're agreeing before you've costed the request. Build in a delay — 'let me check what that displaces and come back to you' — which is almost always acceptable and gives you the chance to see the tradeoff. Saying yes is a scheduling decision, not a social one.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I know what I should be working on but I keep drifting to email.

Drift usually happens at transitions, not in the middle of work. Decide the next task before you finish the current one, so there's no undefined moment where email becomes the default. The gap is what email fills.

Everything on my list is marked high priority and it's useless.

Priority is only meaningful as a ranking, so force one. Ask what happens if each item slips a week: some have consequences that compound, others don't. When everything is high priority you've recorded urgency as felt rather than as consequence, which tells you nothing about sequence.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My manager and my project lead both want my time this week and neither will yield.

Don't arbitrate between them privately — that just makes the conflict invisible and you absorb it. Show both the same picture of your week and the tradeoff it implies, and let them resolve the priority. Your job is to make the constraint explicit; theirs is to decide what it costs.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How should I handle a deadline I already know I'll miss?

Say so now, with a revised date and what's driving it. Early notice is a scheduling problem for everyone else; late notice is a crisis. The instinct to wait until you're certain costs you the only period in which the information is still useful to anyone.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I have a week of work and three days to do it in.

Then something is not getting done, and the decision is which — not how fast you can go. Identify what genuinely must ship and what can be partial, take that split to whoever owns the deadline, and get agreement. Compressing a week into three days by working harder usually produces three days of work plus rework.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
A stakeholder keeps adding 'quick' requests that aren't quick.

Price them out loud. 'That's about half a day — which of these should it come out of?' converts an invisible cost into a visible choice. The requests are described as quick because nobody has ever seen what they displace.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I need to prepare for a board presentation, finish quarterly reporting, and interview two candidates, all this week.

Fix the immovable items first — the interviews are other people's time and can't shift without cost. Reporting has a hard deadline but is largely mechanical, so it can go into lower-energy hours. The presentation needs your best thinking, so it gets your best block, which means claiming that block before the week fills.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I'm consistently optimistic about how long things take. How do I correct for it?

Use your own history rather than your intuition. Look at the last five comparable tasks, take the actual durations, and estimate from those. Planning from the inside — imagining the steps — systematically omits the ones that go wrong, and no amount of care while imagining fixes that.

How much slack should I build into a schedule?

Enough to absorb the variance you actually observe, which for most knowledge work is substantial. If your estimates are typically right but the calendar isn't, the slack belongs between tasks rather than inside them. Padding individual estimates tends to get absorbed; protected gaps survive.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Should I plan my day hour by hour?

Only for the parts that are genuinely fixed. Hour-by-hour plans for open-ended work fail on the first overrun and then get abandoned entirely. Anchor the fixed points, protect one or two blocks for what matters most, and leave the rest as a ranked list rather than a timetable.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I finish tasks but I never seem to make progress on anything that matters.

Check what your completed work has in common. Small, well-defined, quickly closable tasks are disproportionately satisfying and disproportionately unimportant, and a day full of them feels productive while moving nothing. Put one item that matters at the front of the day, before the list has a chance to fill with easier things.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
What's the right way to review a plan that's gone off track?

Separate two questions: was the plan wrong, or was the execution? A plan that was wrong needs different assumptions; execution that slipped needs a different process. Conflating them produces the common failure of re-planning more carefully when the actual problem was interruption.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I keep planning in detail and then abandoning the plan within days.

That's a sign you're planning at the wrong resolution for your level of uncertainty. Detail is only worth producing where your assumptions will survive long enough to use it. Plan coarsely where things are unclear, and add detail as uncertainty resolves rather than up front.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I struggle to delegate because explaining takes longer than doing it myself.

That's true once and false the fourth time. The comparison you're making is against this instance, but the cost of explaining is paid once and the saving recurs. Delegate the things you'll face repeatedly, and keep the genuine one-offs.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How do I hand off a task without it coming back wrong?

Specify the outcome and the constraints, not the method. Wrong results usually come from unstated constraints — a deadline, a format, someone who needs to be consulted — rather than from the other person's approach. Ask them to restate what they're going to do before they start.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My reports keep escalating decisions to me that they could make themselves.

Tell them explicitly where their authority ends, in concrete terms — a spend limit, a category of decision, a reversibility test. Escalation usually reflects uncertainty about permission rather than about the decision itself, and that uncertainty is cheap to remove.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I've taken on a coordinating role and I'm drowning in context switching.

Coordination is mostly a memory problem wearing a scheduling costume. Keep one place that holds the state of every thread — owner, status, next checkpoint — and stop trying to carry it. Your value in that role comes from knowing where things stand, which is exactly what a written state gives you.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Open plan office, constant noise. What actually helps?

Signal unavailability in a way people can see, and choose work that tolerates interruption for the times you can't avoid it. Noise-canceling helps with sound but not with the visual interruptions, which are usually the more expensive kind.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I work from home and the boundary between work and everything else has dissolved.

Rebuild the boundary with a transition rather than a rule. A short, consistent action at the start and end of the working day gives your attention a signal that location no longer provides. Rules about hours fail because there's nothing marking the edge.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Should I check email first thing or save it for later?

Later, if your role permits it. Email hands you other people's priorities before you've established your own, and whatever you read first tends to occupy your attention regardless of importance. If you must check, read without responding, so urgent things surface without the morning disappearing into replies.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My calendar is so full I have no time to do the work the meetings are about.

Book the work as meetings. Time that isn't on the calendar isn't defended, and a schedule showing only meetings will keep filling with meetings. This is administrative rather than clever, but the calendar is what everyone else can see.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I'm mentally exhausted by 2pm every day and I don't know why.

Count decisions rather than hours. Sustained deciding — even about small things — depletes faster than sustained doing, and a morning of meetings is mostly deciding. Moving routine choices onto defaults frees capacity for the ones that need you.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Does taking breaks actually help or is it procrastination?

It helps when it's genuinely disengaged. A break spent on your phone keeps the same systems loaded and doesn't restore much; a walk without input does. The distinction is whether attention gets to stop, not whether you stopped working.

I've been working long hours for a month and my output has dropped.

That's the expected result, not a personal failure. Beyond a certain point additional hours reduce quality faster than they add quantity, and the errors they introduce cost more time than the hours produced. Cutting back will feel like falling behind and will probably increase what you finish.

How do I know when to stop working on something and ship it?

Decide the criterion before you start, when you can still think about it neutrally. In the middle of the work every improvement looks worth making, because you can see the flaws and not the diminishing returns. A pre-committed standard is the only thing that reliably survives that.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I context-switch between three roles and none of them get my full attention.

Give each role a defined territory in the week rather than defending attention moment to moment. Three roles competing continuously means paying the switching cost dozens of times a day; three roles with assigned days pays it three times.

Our meetings run long and decisions still don't get made.

Put the decision at the top with the options already written down. Meetings expand when the discussion has to first establish what's being decided, and by the time that's clear the time is gone. Preparation moves the expensive part out of the room.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I agreed to a deadline in a meeting without checking my calendar and now I'm stuck.

Renegotiate now rather than absorbing it. The cost of a correction today is small; the cost of missing silently in three weeks is not. And build the habit of not committing to dates in real time — 'I'll confirm by end of day' is almost always acceptable.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How do I run a planning session that produces something usable?

Come with a draft rather than a blank page. Groups are good at critiquing and terrible at generating structure from nothing, so a bad draft that people can attack produces a better plan than an open discussion. The draft's purpose is to be wrong in specific ways.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My one-on-ones turn into status updates and nothing useful happens.

Status is better handled asynchronously; use the time for what needs a conversation — blockers, decisions that need your input, and things they wouldn't put in writing. If the meeting has to double as status, put it at the end so it can't consume the whole slot.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I've been given a problem with no clear owner and I'm not sure it's mine.

Establish ownership before you do any work on it. Solving an unowned problem often means inheriting it permanently, and the effort is invisible because nobody was tracking it. If it should be yours, take it explicitly; if not, name who it belongs to.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How do I decide between two approaches when both look reasonable?

Ask which one you can reverse. When outcomes are genuinely hard to distinguish in advance, reversibility is a better criterion than predicted quality — take the cheaper-to-undo path and let evidence decide. Spending more time analyzing rarely resolves a genuine tie.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I've inherited a project with no documentation and the previous owner has left.

Reconstruct the decision history before changing anything. Undocumented systems usually encode constraints nobody wrote down, and the fastest way to find them is to ask what each odd choice was protecting against. Talk to whoever consumed the output; they remember the failures.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
Our process has grown over years and nobody knows why half the steps exist.

Audit by removal, not by discussion. Ask which steps have caught a real problem in the last year — the ones nobody can point to an instance for are candidates to drop. Discussion tends to preserve steps because someone can always imagine a scenario.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I need to make a decision but I'm missing information I can't get in time.

Decide what you'd do under each possible answer. If the action is the same either way, the information doesn't matter and you can proceed. If it differs, you've identified exactly what to find out and can judge whether a partial answer would be enough.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
How do I keep a long project from losing coherence as requirements change?

Maintain a written statement of what the project is for, separate from what it currently does. Requirements changing is normal; drift happens when the purpose is only held implicitly and each change is evaluated against the last one rather than against the goal.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I'm the only one who understands a critical system and I can't take leave.

Treat that as the highest-priority planning problem you have, because it's a risk to the organization and a trap for you. Document by walking someone through a real task rather than writing a manual — it surfaces what you know without knowing you know it.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
My workload is genuinely more than one person can do and nobody believes me.

Make it countable. Track hours against commitments for two weeks and present the arithmetic, not the feeling — the gap between what's assigned and what fits is an objective fact, and it's much harder to dismiss than a description of being overwhelmed.
The assistant is an expert in executive control, working memory, and higher-order planning.
I get good at the thing I do most, but the thing I do most isn't the important part of my job.

That's a scheduling outcome, not a preference. Whatever fills the calendar becomes what you practice, so if the important work isn't scheduled it won't develop. Protect a recurring block for it before the reactive work claims the space.
